claims.text: For HEAs with identical compositions and heat treatments, synthesis route governs hardness and strength.
Synthesis route governs hardness and strength by controlling cooling rate.
Cooling rate determines formation of a refined microstructure containing nanoscale precipitates and particular grain-boundary configurations.
Nanoscale precipitates and grain boundaries act as barriers to dislocation motion.
The controlled comparison uses specimens of the same HEA composition produced by a high-cooling-rate route and a slower-cooling-rate route.
Additive manufacturing is proposed as the high-cooling-rate route.
Traditional casting or deposition is proposed as the slower-cooling-rate route.
Both specimen sets receive identical post-processing heat treatments, while composition and alloy purity are held constant.
Rapid solidification in the additive-manufacturing route forms grain boundaries and nanoscale precipitates.
High cooling rates promote rapid nucleation and consequently finer grain sizes.
High cooling rates produce a high density of nanoscale precipitates.
Finer grains and a high density of nanoscale precipitates provide more effective obstacles to dislocation motion.
Slower-cooled cast material has a coarser microstructure with fewer obstacles to dislocation motion.
The high-cooling-rate specimens will have greater hardness than the slower-cooled cast baseline.
The high-cooling-rate specimens will have greater yield strength than the slower-cooled cast baseline.
The predicted increases in hardness and yield strength correspond to finer grains and higher densities of grain boundaries and nanoscale precipitates.

The hypothesis is limited to compositions and processing regimes in which cooling rate dominates microstructural refinement and may fail when post-deposition deformation or other processing parameters substantially modify the microstructure.

Failure of the additively manufactured specimens to show statistically significant grain refinement, increased precipitate density, and corresponding hardness and yield-strength increases relative to cast specimens would falsify the proposed mechanism.
